title: His play
hook: all happens within His will and His play

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 11: karan kaaran, the doer and the cause of causes. Your line was he is the doer. Did you loosen your grip on one outcome? Today, the first stanza. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

Rain on the morning of the wedding. A flight canceled. The diagnosis nobody wanted. A baby who arrives three weeks early, on the one day everyone was away. Every life has moments when the plan simply doesn't happen, and nothing you could have done would have changed it. Some people rage. Some people go numb. And in many Sikh homes, you'll hear an elder say a short phrase, quietly, sometimes through tears: bhaana mannana. Accept the will. It isn't giving up. It's something harder. The first stanza of ashtpadi eleven is where that phrase comes from.
screen: `RAIN ON THE WEDDING DAY.` → `NOTHING YOU COULD HAVE DONE.` → `BHAANA MANNANA: ACCEPT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: The stanza begins: God is able to do, and to have things done. Then: jo tis bhaavai soee hog. Whatever pleases Him, that comes to pass. Bhaavai is the root of bhaana, the will, what is pleasing to God. Then the pictures arrive fast. In an instant He sets up and takes down. By His order He holds the earth up with no support beneath it. By His order things are born, and by His order they merge back. High and low, every shade and form, all by His order. And then: He makes and makes, and beholds His own greatness. Nanak, He is pervading all. Read that and you might picture a stern ruler issuing commands. But Sukhmani, in other places, uses a gentler word for the whole show: khel, play. Like a child building a sandcastle, delighting in it, and letting the tide take it, and building again. The creation is God's play, made with delight and watched with delight. Put the two together, the will and the play, and you get the heart of bhaana mannana. Accepting the will isn't accepting that someone up there is cruel. It's trusting that even the rain on the wedding day is inside a play made with love, though we can't see the whole stage. And here's the careful part: Sikhs who accept the bhaana still grieve, still fight injustice, still call the doctor. Acceptance is about what you can't change. Tomorrow, the stanzas go one step further.
screen: `JO TIS BHAAVAI: WHATEVER PLEASES HIM.` · `SET UP AND TAKEN DOWN IN AN INSTANT.` · `KHEL: CREATION AS PLAY.` · `ACCEPTANCE, NOT GIVING UP.` · then, large: `HIS WILL.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept one thing you can't change. Find one. Not something you can still work on, but something truly fixed: the weather, a past event, someone else's choice, a loss. Hold it in mind. Notice where you push against it in your body: the jaw, the stomach, the shoulders. Breathe into that place. You don't have to like it. Just let it be what it is, inside the play. If you pray, you can say the two words many Sikhs say: bhaana mannana. The bell holds the time.
His play. Jo tis bhaavai soee hog: whatever pleases Him comes to pass, and the whole creation is His play, made and watched with delight.
Your line: his will. Today, when something you can't change goes wrong, breathe once, say the line, and then do the next thing you can do. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs speak of 'bhaana mannana', accepting God's will, especially in grief or hardship, while still working to change what can be changed.

original.note: Gurmukhi: khel, play; Sukhmani pictures the creation as God's play, made and watched with delight.

trapdoor: what you thought: accepting God's will means giving up.
what it means: it means trusting a play made with love, even when you can't see the whole stage, and still doing your part.
what a scholar hears: bhaana derives from bhaavai (what pleases); 'bhaana mannana' is a core Sikh ethic of acceptance, held with the duty to resist injustice.
